title: The Oregon Supervised Practice Portfolio Examination (final rules as approved by the Oregon Supreme Court, 7 November 2023)
pub: Oregon State Bar / Oregon Supreme Court
author: Oregon State Board of Bar Examiners · Oregon Supreme Court

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Reliable delivery: Legal engineering bridges capability and service
st.an: The source sets procedural rules for Oregon’s supervised-practice admission pathway and accommodations. It does not address AI capability, legal engineering, verification, task-specific evaluation, service redesign or AI-enabled legal-service delivery, so its position relative to the cluster proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source establishes detailed supervision, assessment, feedback and workload rules for provisional legal practice, which is adjacent to the cluster’s concern with preserving professional development. However, it does not address legal AI, jagged capability, verification, selective deployment or AI-driven work redesign, so its position on the cluster’s proposition cannot be determined.

st.t: Licensed alternatives: Expanded practice retains accountability
st.an: The Oregon rules directly support the cluster’s proposition that alternative entry can retain licensing, competence assessment, accountable supervision and client safeguards. They establish a practice-based portfolio route while preserving character-and-fitness review, insurance, supervisory responsibility, automatic suspension and client-protection duties. They prescribe a regulatory design and quality-control process rather than demonstrating improved access or competence outcomes.

mo.t: AI insurance: Exclusions operate beyond negligent hallucinations
AI supervision: Retained responsibility is not strict liability
Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs

kp.k: Supervised practice offers an alternative route to bar admission
kp.d: The rules approved on 7 November 2023 establish the SPPE as a means of demonstrating minimum competence without taking the Uniform Bar Examination or, through an alternative professional-responsibility assessment, the MPRE. Other admission requirements remain applicable, including character and fitness. This is a regulatory framework for professional formation, not evidence that AI caused the reform.
qs: The Oregon Supervised Practice Portfolio Examination (SPPE) offers an avenue for establishing minimum competence to practice law.
Those candidates, however, must satisfy all other requirements specified in the Rules for Admission.

kp.k: AI-assisted submissions require disclosure and identifiable personal contributions
kp.d: Rule 6.4 expressly accommodates written work founded on AI compositions, templates or forms. Candidates must disclose assistance, submit the original foundation, highlight their additions or modifications, and avoid reusing the same foundation for multiple submissions. Only their additions, edits or customization count toward the applicable word-count requirements. These provisions govern attribution in competence assessment rather than prohibit AI use.
qs: the extent to which the Licensee relied upon artificial intelligence programs
The Provisional Licensee must highlight the portions of the work product that represent the Provisional Licensee’s additions, edits, or other customization;
The Provisional Licensee may not rely upon the same template, form, or artificial intelligence text for more than one work product submitted to the Examiners;

kp.k: Supervisors attest accuracy and assessability of assisted work
kp.d: For each written submission, the supervising attorney must review the candidate's disclosed assistance and attest that the work sufficiently reflects the candidate's own research, analysis and writing to support meaningful assessment. The supervisor must also attest to accurate legal analysis and identify whether and how the employer used the work. This separates responsibility for accuracy from examiners' evaluation of competence.
qs: Attest that, after reviewing the assistance noted by the Provisional Licensee on their cover sheet, the work product sufficiently reflects the knowledge/research, analysis, and writing of the Provisional Licensee that BBX can meaningfully assess the Provisional Licensee’s competence from the work product;
Attest that the legal analysis is accurate;
Indicate if and how the Employer used the work product.

kp.k: Qualification combines documented practice hours and demonstrated skills
kp.d: Candidates must document at least 675 program hours, submit at least eight written work products, lead two client interviews or counseling sessions, and conduct two negotiations. At least three written pieces must be at least 1500 words, excluding headers and signature blocks but including footnotes. Qualifying hours include legal work, program components and employer-required education; up to 100 hours of JD-stage legal work can count subject to specified supervision, certification and recordkeeping conditions.
qs: To demonstrate their minimum competence and qualify for admission to the Oregon State Bar, Provisional Licensees must document at least 675 hours spent working within the Supervised Practice Program.
Each Provisional Licensee must prepare and submit at least 8 pieces of written work product.
At least 3 of the 8 pieces of work product must be at least 1500 words long, not including headers or signature blocks.
Each Provisional Licensee must lead two client interviews or counseling sessions that are assessed by their Supervising Attorney.
Each Provisional Licensee must conduct two negotiations that are assessed by the Supervising Attorney.

kp.k: Client interaction and negotiation require candidate leadership
kp.d: The rules require supervisor assessment and feedback on actual candidate-led interviewing, counseling and negotiation, with little or no supervisory assistance during the assessed performance. Written exchanges can qualify alongside oral interactions. Mock written work and approved simulations provide alternatives when ordinary supervised practice cannot supply the required experiences.
qs: The rubric will include an attestation that the Provisional Licensee led the interview or counseling session, with little or no assistance from the Supervising Attorney.
The rubric will include an attestation that the Provisional Licensee led the negotiation, with little or no assistance from the Supervising Attorney.

If the Provisional Licensee is unable to gather sufficient work product from client-related work, the Supervising Attorney may assign a mock exercise or exercises to the Provisional Licensee, which can be submitted to fulfill this requirement.

kp.k: Employers and supervisors carry substantial professional formation duties
kp.d: Employers generally must provide at least 20 hours of paid work weekly and salary and benefits comparable to other recent law graduates, with grant, stipend and unbilled pro bono exceptions. They must provide tools and training access and accommodate completion of program requirements. Supervisors must provide regular feedback and retain professional responsibility even when delegating supervision to another qualified Oregon lawyer.
qs: Include Provisional Licensees in any training programs or other educational activities provided to other new lawyers working for the Employer;
Provide other regular feedback that will help the Provisional Licensee develop their skills and better serve Employer clients.

The Supervising Attorney, however, retains professional responsibility for the work of the Provisional Licensee and the supervisory competence of the lawyer to whom they delegate any supervisory duties.

kp.k: Ethical competence can be demonstrated through reflective practice
kp.d: Candidates may establish professional-responsibility competence with an MPRE score of at least 85 or, after passing a law-school Professional Responsibility course, ten journal entries independently assessed by an examiner. Entries must analyze lawyering situations using relevant Oregon professional-conduct rules and cover at least five of their eight chapters. Consultation with colleagues and ethics resources is expressly encouraged.
qs: Achieving a score of at least 85 on the Multistate Professional Responsibility Exam (MPRE);
The journal entries should discuss rules drawn from at least 5 of the 8 chapters of the Oregon Rules of Professional Conduct.
Provisional Licensees may discuss the issues they write about with colleagues, the State Bar’s Legal Ethics Hotline, and other sources.
An Examiner will independently assess the content of the journal entries submitted under option (2).

kp.k: Training includes practice management, inclusion and access to justice
kp.d: Candidates must complete all 15 hours of the PLF's most recent Learning the Ropes program and at least ten hours related to diversity, equity, inclusion or access to justice. The latter may include pro bono work, MCLE, affinity-bar volunteering or approved self-study; it is not an exclusively access-to-justice requirement. Supervisors and examiners must also complete at least two hours of program-related diversity, equity and inclusion training.
qs: Provisional Licensees must devote at least 10 hours to activities related to diversity, equity, inclusion, or access to justice.
These activities may include pro bono work, MCLE programs, volunteer work with affinity bar associations, and self-study.
The Provisional Licensee must attend or watch all 15 hours of the most recent “Learning the Ropes” program offered by the Oregon State Bar Professional Liability Fund.

kp.k: Portfolio assessment uses anonymous grading and iterative feedback
kp.d: A required halfway portfolio follows 350 hours of program work. Examiners use published rubrics and qualified/not-qualified judgments, with multiple examiners participating over time and two grading each written piece where practicable. Qualified components carry forward; unsuccessful components require new work rather than revisions. Final portfolio submissions are unlimited, but assessed writing, interviewing/counseling and negotiation components are subject to the stated three-calendar-year scoring window.
qs: All Portfolios will be graded anonymously.
If practicable, at least two Examiners will grade each piece of written work product (Rule 6.4) included in a Portfolio.
The replacement component must be a new piece of work, not a revised version of the original submission.
There is no limit on the number of Final Portfolios that a Provisional Licensee may submit.

kp.k: Client protection constrains practice and portfolio construction
kp.d: Client needs take priority over program completion. Written client work requires protective redaction and client consent before portfolio inclusion. Employers must arrange professional-liability coverage unless exempt; exemptions include specified in-house, government, public-defense and legal-aid practice. Loss of required insurance or an approved supervisor automatically suspends the provisional license.
qs: The needs of clients must take precedence over completing the requirements of the Program.
The work product must be redacted to protect the client’s interests;
The client must consent to inclusion of the work product in the Portfolio.

During any period for which the Provisional Licensee lacks a Supervising Attorney approved by Regulatory Counsel, the Provisional Licensee’s license shall be immediately and automatically suspended under Section 16.

kp.k: Program evaluation is mandated rather than demonstrated
kp.d: The rules require annual scoring-consistency checks, reviews of whether completed portfolios demonstrate minimum competence, and participant feedback. At least every other year, the Board must collect practice-area, employer, client and salary data, alongside malpractice-claim and bar-complaint data concerning program licensees. Annual reporting and four-year Supreme Court reauthorization provide continuing oversight; the document supplies no results from these evaluations.
qs: At least once a year, the Board will randomly select several completed Portfolios to assess whether those Portfolios—taken as a whole— demonstrate minimum competence to practice law.
The Board will also gather data on malpractice claims and bar complaints against individuals licensed through the program.
Every fourth year, the Court will vote whether to re-authorize the Program.

kp.k: Early uptake depends on employers supplying supervised opportunities
kp.d: The appended ABA Journal report of 13 June 2024 records 47 candidate applications and applications from 62 attorneys at 57 employers as of June 10, following a May 15 opening. These are application counts, not admissions or completed placements. Gallini describes the route as market-driven because it requires willing supervisors and employers. The report states that eligibility is not confined to Oregon graduates or recent graduates.
qs: As of June 10, 47 candidates had applied to take that pathway, and 62 attorneys from 57 employers have applied to supervise a candidate, Kateri Walsh, Oregon State Bar director of communications, told the ABA Journal.
Applications opened May 15.
Candidacy is not limited to in-state graduates and there is no time limit on when they have graduated.
If there are no employers who raise their hand and say, ‘I will be a supervising attorney,’ then there’s no pathway to licensure. This would never get off the ground.

kp.k: Supporters emphasize competence; early licensing evidence remains limited
kp.d: In the ABA Journal excerpt, law-school dean Tamara F. Lawson argues that supervised practice is more closely connected to competence than multiple-choice testing; this is her assessment, not a reported comparative study. The Lewis & Clark update dated 24 February 2025 states that four of the first five licensed attorneys were its graduates, establishing initial completions without supplying comparative competence or client-outcome evidence.
qs: “It is strange that the legal profession allows you to go to school, take a bunch of tests while in school and after school and never talk to a client—and that’s our current model,” says Tamara F. Lawson, dean of the University of Washington School of Law.
Supervised practice “is more closely linked to competence than any 100 multiple-choice questions will ever be.”
Four of the first five attorneys who earned their licenses are L&C grads.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The Oregon SPPE rules accommodate AI-assisted legal writing in competence portfolios, subject to disclosure, identification of the candidate’s own contribution, and supervisory attestations.
pts.d: The Oregon State Board of Bar Examiners’ rules, approved by the Oregon Supreme Court, establish an operational treatment of AI-assisted work rather than predicting AI’s effects on employment, productivity, or legal markets. Rule 6.4 requires disclosure of AI reliance. Where AI text provides the foundation for a submission, candidates must supply that text and highlight their own changes; only those changes count toward word-count requirements, and the same foundation cannot support multiple submissions. Supervisors must attest both that the work permits meaningful assessment of the candidate’s competence and that its legal analysis is accurate. This preserves a distinction between evaluating the candidate’s competence and checking the accuracy of the submitted analysis.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The basis is regulatory authority, not empirical evidence about AI’s performance or effects.
pts.d: Rules 6.4 and 9.3 document how AI-assisted submissions are to be handled in this admission pathway. The document supplies no AI benchmarks, measured accuracy rates, productivity findings, or AI-specific participant outcomes. The appended 2024 application figures and 2025 licensing report concern uptake and completion of the SPPE generally; they do not establish use or effects of AI.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: These are requirements in the rules approved on 7 November 2023, applicable to SPPE portfolio submissions rather than a forecast of future AI adoption.
pts.d: Disclosure applies to AI reliance in submitted written work. The additional provenance and contribution requirements apply specifically when an AI composition is used as the foundation. Candidates must attest to the accuracy of their cover-sheet disclosures, and supervisors must confirm assessability and accurate legal analysis. The rules specify no AI-driven transformation timeline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The direct effects concern provisional licensees, supervising attorneys, and portfolio examiners; client-related submissions also require redaction and consent.
pts.d: Candidates using AI must document its contribution and distinguish their own work. Supervising attorneys bear attestation and supervision responsibilities, while examiners assess competence using the work, disclosures, and attestations. For client matters, the general portfolio safeguards apply whether or not AI was used. These are not stated as AI-specific client-consent requirements, nor does the source claim that AI improves access to justice or lowers client costs.
